result:
The proposed answer of 171 matches my own derivation of the lower bound and appears achievable, though I did not fully verify the construction.

**Setup.** Ana can fail to separate primes p and q exactly when some response R is consistent with both periods and comes from a nonconstant function. A response consistent with period p must be constant on each class of "same residue mod p" among the queried points. Being consistent with both p and q means R is constant on the classes of the join of the two relations. The join's classes are the connected components of the bipartite graph whose vertices are the queried residues mod p and mod q, with one edge per query point.

- If the join has at least 2 classes, give the classes different values. This R is consistent with both periods and nonconstant, so p and q cannot be told apart.
- If the join has exactly 1 class, R must be constant. A constant R is consistent with period p only if some residue mod p is unqueried, since Banana's function must be nonconstant. So p and q are separated exactly when one of them has all its residues queried.

**Lower bound.** For every pair of primes, the graph must be connected. At most one prime can have an unqueried residue. Let S be the set of primes with an unqueried residue, so |S| ≤ 1.

- Every prime outside S has all its residues queried. A pair of such primes (p, q) then has p + q vertices, and connectivity needs at least p + q − 1 edges. Each query point gives one edge, so n ≥ p + q − 1.
- The best choice is S = {97}, leaving 83 and 89 as the two largest fully covered primes. This gives n ≥ 83 + 89 − 1 = 171.
- Other choices are worse: S = {89} gives 179, and S = {83} or S = ∅ gives 185.

So n ≥ 171.

**Sufficiency.** Take 171 points whose residues mod 83 and mod 89 form a spanning tree on 83 + 89 vertices. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the residues mod the other primes can be chosen independently for each prime. For each other prime, the residue assignment must make its graph with every other prime connected. This looks feasible with 171 edges and few vertices. The solution only asserts it, but I found no obstruction.

The final answer of 171 is correct.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
